title: Chapter 164 – The Quiet Boy
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Bell]

Bell keeps her own ledger now.

It is not a fine one. It is a sheet of rough paper folded into a book, tied with a thread, and she keeps it in the pocket of her smock beside the reed and the flask. In the first column she writes the hour. In the second, the name of the patient. In the third, the number she has learned to dread: the pulses she counts at each bedside, one after another, down the long cold terraces of the Hall.

She walks the rounds at dawn and at dusk. Nurse showed her the way on the first day, along the ring of light and down the spiral stair, and now she can do it in the dark. Terrace one. Terrace two. The long blue rows of sleepers, row after row, bed after bed, each with its small brass number, each breathing in the slow regular rhythm of the very deeply asleep. She does not touch them all. There are two hundred thousand, and she has two hands. She touches the ones that Nurse marks with a chalk cross on the rail, the ones whose pulses have begun to skip.

Today there are forty-one crosses.

She walks the first terrace with Yue behind her, the girl's palm flat against the rail, her eyes on the floor. Yue has become a good nurse in a week. She has the patience, and the stillness, and a way of laying two fingers on a wrist that makes even the dying seem to settle. They do not speak. They have no need. When Bell reaches the cross-marked bed, she kneels and takes the wrist and counts, and Yue kneels at the other side and takes the other, and they look at each other across the sleeper's body and nod.

Forty-one crosses. They find thirty-six still breathing.

Bell writes the five names in her book and does not let herself count them.

* * *

The wake of Hai Ren is set for the ninth day after the last.

Eight days have passed. They have been, Bell thinks, the strangest eight days of her life. Zhen Li has lit ninety-one lamps. Ninety-one fixtures along the ring and the spokes and the stair, each one now burning with a small amber flame that the Hall's cold blue light cannot quite drown. The corridors are warmer. The air smells of hot brass. In the mornings he sits on the floor of the Annex with the tarnished lamp in his lap, and Nurse brings him tea, and he drinks it without a word.

He has lost things. She has watched him lose them. On the third day he forgot the name of the village where he was born. On the fifth he stopped whistling, though he does not seem to know he ever did. On the seventh he looked at the stove in the corner of the Annex and said, in a puzzled voice, "That's a nice color," and Bell realized that he could no longer remember what apples smelled like.

She told Jian. Jian said nothing for a long time. Then he said, very quietly, "He will not stop."

"No."

"And I cannot ask him to."

"No," said Bell. "But you can ask him what he would like to keep."

Jian did. Zhen Li considered the question with grave attention, sitting cross-legged on the cot with the lamp warm in his hands. Then he said, "I'd like to keep Ao's laugh. And Mo Yan's drawings. And Nurse's tea." A pause. "And the face of the man who used to hold the other end of the ladder."

"Your father?"

"Is that what he was?" said Zhen Li, curiously. And Bell had to turn away.

* * *

Ao catches her sleeve in the corridor the night before.

He is wearing the duck-hemmed gown, which Nurse has let down twice, and he is carrying the rabbit by one ear. His face is solemn. He looks up at Bell with the stern, unblinking expression of a very small judge, and says, "Is Hai Ren going to be sad?"

She crouches. "Why do you ask?"

"Because he never talked." He thinks. "When I was awake, the first time, before I went to sleep. I was in the room with him. All the big ones were quiet. But he was the quietest. He sat by the window and didn't say anything for a whole day, and then he said, 'I am waiting.'"

"Waiting for what?"

"I don't know." Ao frowns. "I think he was waiting to be sad. Like when you wait for a sneeze."

Bell has to look away for a moment.

"Perhaps," she says. "Perhaps he is. But he has a lot of friends now. You, and Tao, and Mo Yan. I think that will help."

"Can I give him the rabbit?"

"Oh, sweetheart."

"Only to hold." He holds it up, with great seriousness. "It's very good for sad. It has a lot of stitches."

She takes the rabbit in both hands, and finds that she cannot answer, and so she nods. Ao pats her arm, satisfied, and runs off down the corridor, and she stands there for a while with the old patched toy against her chest.

* * *

The Quiet School teaches that the worst thing a man can do is to move without reason.

She has this from Ethan, who relays it through the grille on the morning of the wake in the slow, dry voice of a scholar reading from a text. The Quiet School was a monastic order, he says, on the high plateaus of a place that no longer exists. Its disciples were taught to sit for years without speaking, to breathe so slowly that a feather held to the lip would not stir. They called this the Great Stillness. They believed that every act, every word, every step, was a small wound in the world, and that a man who could stop acting could stop wounding.

I chose Hai Ren, says Ethan, because he was the best they had.

"Chose him for what?" Bell asks.

For the seal. A long pause. A copy needs a child who can hold still while it settles. Most children fight. Hai Ren simply... waited. I have never met a boy more patient. He was fourteen. He had been in the Quiet School for nine years.

Bell looks through the grille at the dim shaft. "And now?"

Now I think he is going to be very unhappy, says Ethan. To wake, after so long. To find that his stillness was not enough.

She says nothing. She stands in the little round room with the slate in her hand and thinks of a boy of fourteen who has spent nine years learning not to wound the world, and who is about to be woken into a Hall where thirty-one beds went quiet in a night.

Be kind to him, says Ethan. Please. He will want to be.

* * *

Zhen Li is on the floor of the Annex when she returns, with his lamp in his lap and a bowl of tea going cold at his knee.

He is not lighting anything. He is only sitting, with his back against the wall, and turning the brass lamp over in his hands, slowly, as if looking for the place where it joins. His face is white. When Bell crouches in front of him, he looks up with an expression of polite, remote curiosity, like a man who has been asked a question in a language he half remembers.

"Are you well?" she asks.

"Yes."

"You forgot something."

"I always forget something." He sets the lamp down. "Today it was the name of a flower. The little white one that grows by the stream. I could see it, but there was no word." He frowns. "Is that a bad one? I can't tell."

"I do not know."

"Neither do I." He picks up the tea and looks at it. "Nurse says I'm a very brave boy. But I think I'm only a boy who doesn't know what he's missing. Is that the same?"

Bell sits down on the floor beside him, with her back to the wall. She is tired to the marrow. She puts her arm round his thin shoulders, and he leans against her, warm and light, with the lamp between them glowing faintly orange.

"No," she says. "It is not the same. But it is close enough that I would not tell Nurse."

He smiles. It is a real smile, small and dry.

"Thank you," he says. "I'll try to remember that."

* * *

The wake is the quietest of all.

She stands at the foot of the cot with the flask in her hand. The ring of light rises from the rail and turns, white and slow. Mei's voice, thin as a thread, whispers from the grille that it is all right, that it hurts less than the last one, that she has been practicing. The sleeping boy in the bed is tall and thin, with long hands and a shaved head and a gray cotton robe that has been mended at the cuffs. His face is calm. It is the calmest face Bell has ever seen on a sleeper.

When he wakes, he does not open his eyes.

She watches for it. A flutter, a twitch, a gasp. There is nothing. The ring of light fades. The hum goes out of the floor. Mei whispers Fourteen, and there is a small sad sound in the wall, and Bell realizes it is Ethan weeping. But the boy on the cot lies still, with his hands folded on his chest, and does not move.

"Is he—" Nurse whispers.

"He is awake," says Bell.

She knows it as she knows her own name. It is in the set of the mouth. In the faint wrinkle between the brows. In the way the long hands, folded on the chest, are not quite relaxed.

"Hai Ren," she says quietly. "You can open your eyes. We're friends."

Nothing.

"There's no one here who means you harm. There are children. There are people who love them. There is a woman named Nurse who has kept you for a very long time, and she is standing right here."

A long pause.

"I know," says the boy.

His voice is a whisper. It is dry and light and utterly without alarm, and it comes from a mouth that does not seem to move.

"I have been listening for a while," says Hai Ren. "I did not wish to disturb you."

* * *

He opens his eyes only when Nurse touches his hand.

They are very dark, almost black, with a steady, patient depth that unsettles Bell more than she would like to say. He looks up at the high curved ceiling, and the amber lamps along the wall, and the pale faces gathered at the foot of the bed. He sits up slowly, with the care of a man easing himself into cold water. He lets the blanket fall.

"I have slept a long time," he says.

"Six hundred years," says Nurse.

"Yes." He does not seem surprised. "I could feel it. The world went by like a river, and I sat on the bank." He turns his head. His gaze goes to the other cots, to the sleepers, and then to the three children huddled by the stove, the two small ones and the silent girl with her charcoal. Something moves in his face. It is so slight that Bell would have missed it if she were not looking.

"They are awake," he says.

"Three of them. And Zhen Li, over there with the lamp. You are the fifth."

"I see." He folds his hands in his lap. "Thank you for waking me. I do not wish to be a burden."

"You are not a burden."

"I have been one." The words are quiet. "I think all of us have been. I have felt the Hall dimming. I have felt what it cost to bring the others up. I have lain here and listened to a ledger being written." He lifts his eyes to Bell. "I would like to be useful, if you will allow it. It is the only way I know to repay a debt."

Bell stares at him. She has delivered nine hundred infants and set bones in the dark and sat with the dying, and she has never met a boy of fourteen who spoke like this.

"Rest first," she says, gruffly. "We can talk about debts later."

"As you wish." He bows his head. "But I have been listening, and I think there is not much later."

* * *

Jian catches her in the corridor before the evening rounds.

He has not slept. She sees it at once, in the gray of his skin and the set of his mouth. He is leaning on the staff outside the Annex, and when she comes out with her satchel he steps into her path and says, quietly, "He has asked to see the terraces."

"He has."

"I would rather he did not."

"So would I." She shifts the satchel on her hip. "He has been awake for a day. He has not eaten what I gave him. He speaks like a man of eighty and sits like a stone. I do not know what he intends, Jian. I know only that he asked."

"He asked because he wishes to be useful." His voice is rough. "That is not the same as wishing to go. We have woken three children in as many weeks, and each time the Hall has taken its price. I do not want to give it a fourth for nothing."

"And if he can help the sleepers?"

"Then he should be asked what he is willing to give." He draws a breath. "I used Ao. I used Tao. I used Mo Yan. I told myself I was asking, but they are children, Bell. They say yes because they want to be good."

She looks at him. His eyes are bright and sunken. His fingers are tight on the staff.

"Then tell him," she says. "Tell him what it may cost. Tell him he may say no."

"I will."

"Good." She softens. "But I am going to take him down, whatever he says. If it is only to look, I would rather it was with me."

He nods slowly. The staff taps once on the floor.

"Be careful," he says.

* * *

He asks to see the terraces that evening.

Bell does not want to take him. She says so. She says he has barely sat up, that his legs are weak, that she will not have a boy who has just woken from six centuries of sleep walking miles of cold stairs. Hai Ren listens to all of it with perfect courtesy and then says, in the same dry whisper, "I do not need my legs. I would like to see them with my hands."

So they take him.

Yue carries the lamp. Zhen Li, white-faced, walks beside the boy with his own brass lantern clenched in his fist. Bell goes last, with her satchel on her hip and her book in her pocket. They go down the long spiral together, past the eighth terrace and the ninth, into the cold blue dark.

Hai Ren stops at the first row.

He stands for a time without moving. Bell has been in the room with a dozen holy men, and none of them could stand like this. It is not rigid. It is not tense. It is simply the stillness of a stone in a river, perfectly in place, letting the water pass. His head is tilted. His long hands hang at his sides. Around his feet, the faint blue glow of the beds seems to quiet, bed by bed, in a ring.

"They are frightened," he says.

"The sleepers?" Bell asks.

"Yes. All of them." His voice is soft. "They do not know it. They are very deep. But under the sleep there is a fear, and it has been growing. It is like a draft in a house. They feel the Hall failing, and they cannot wake, and so they hold their breath."

He kneels. He lays his hand on the nearest sleeper's brow.

It is a stranger: a stout middle-aged man in a gray tunic, with a gray beard and a face drawn with age. Bell had not noted him before. His pulse is thirty-eight. It is slow, and shallow, and as Hai Ren touches him she sees the muscles of the man's face, which have been clenched for six hundred years, begin to loosen.

"There," whispers the boy. "There. You can let go."

The stout man exhales.

It is a long breath, a sigh that seems to go on for a minute, and as it leaves him the faint blue light around the bed dims and goes out. The pulse beneath Bell's fingers slows, and slows, and stops.

She looks up, appalled.

"What did you do?"

"I let him rest." Hai Ren's dark eyes are calm. "He was in pain. He has been in pain for a very long time. The Great Stillness does not heal. It only stops the falling. I have stopped it for him, so that he may go without fear."

* * *

She cannot speak for a long time.

She stands at the end of the row with her hand over her mouth and watches the boy move from bed to bed. A touch on the brow. A breath. A sigh, a dimming, a stillness. Forty-one crosses on the rails, and he goes to each of them. He does not hurry. He does not look away. At each cot he kneels and lays his hand on the sleeper's forehead and says something, so softly that Bell cannot hear, and then the sleeper breathes out, once, and is gone.

She does not stop him.

She tells herself that she should. She tells herself that this is not what the wake was for, that he was brought up to live, not to be a death's-head in a gray robe. But the faces of the dead are smooth. The faces of the dead are calm. There is no pain in them. They look, she thinks, as if they were sleeping for the first time in six hundred years.

Beside her, Yue is crying silently. She has her palm pressed flat against the floor. She feels it, Bell realizes: the passing, the long soft letting-go, a shudder running through the boards from bed to bed.

At the thirtieth cross, Hai Ren stops.

He sways. His hand is still on the sleeper's brow, but his shoulders have begun to shake, a fine fierce trembling that runs the length of his thin frame. His breath comes shallow. A line of sweat stands on his lip.

"Hai Ren," Bell says, sharply. "That is enough."

"Not yet."

"You are shaking."

"It costs." He does not turn. "Every one costs. It is the Stillness. It takes from me what it gives to them." A pause. "I have given thirty. I should like to give the eleven."

"Stop."

"I cannot." His voice is steady, very soft. "They would be afraid."

Bell starts toward him. A hand catches her sleeve. Yue is shaking her head, slowly, her face wet, and Bell understands, with a terrible clarity, that the girl is feeling every death in the floor, and every breath of the boy, and that she is telling her it is all right.

She stops. She stands with her hand clenched in her smock and watches the boy finish.

* * *

It takes him until midnight.

When he has done the last of them, he falls. Bell catches him before he strikes the floor, and the weight of him is nothing, a bundle of sticks in a gray robe. His head lolls on her arm. His eyes are open, black and clear, and they find her face and hold.

"Is it done?" he whispers.

"It is done."

"Good." A faint smile. "I am glad. I did not wish to leave any frightened."

She lays two fingers on his throat. The pulse is thready, fast, and wrong. She feels it skip.

"I am going to carry you back," she says. "And you are going to lie down, and I am going to watch you, and you are not going to move for two days. Do you understand?"

"I will try."

"You will do it."

"Yes." The faint smile deepens. "You remind me of my teacher."

She lifts him in her arms. He weighs less than a child. Behind her, Yue is lighting the way with Zhen Li's lantern, and the amber glow falls along the long blue rows of sleepers, over the forty-one beds where the rails have gone dark. Bell walks up the stair with the boy in her arms and does not look at them.

On the eighth terrace she stops for breath, and finds that the book in her pocket is wet.

She takes it out. The page has been soaked through. Her tears, she thinks, then sees that it is not. It is the ink. The numbers she wrote at dawn have run together, blurred, become a gray smear. The forty-one crosses are gone. The names are gone. Only the last line is still legible, in her own cramped hand.

Forty-one. Thirty-six breathing at first count.

She closes the book. She holds the boy a little tighter. And she climbs, one stair at a time, toward the lamps.

* * *

Nurse is at the lectern when she comes down for the dawn round.

The cracked blue ledger lies open under the lamp, and Nurse stands over it with the stub of brown ink in her hand. She has not slept either. Her round face is gray, and there are creases in it that Bell has not seen before. She does not look up when Bell stops beside her.

"Forty-one," Nurse says.

"Yes."

"I have written the numbers. The bed numbers." Her voice is flat. "I have the date. I have the time. It is the column in the middle that troubles me. I have written one word in it for six hundred years."

Bell looks down at the page. The first line is blank, a gap in the ruled column where the word should be. She sees the pen has hovered there, once, twice, and left a faint blot.

"Gone," says Nurse. "It is the word. I wrote it for the first sleeper I lost, and I have written it ever since. I never gave it a thought. Now I look at it, and I do not think it is true."

"What would you write?"

"I do not know." Nurse's mouth tightens. "These forty-one were not taken. They were not stolen by the dark or by the failing of the Gate. They were released. Someone sat with each and told them that they might go." She lifts the pen. "I do not know a word for that."

Bell thinks of the boy in the gray robe. Of the stout man's long breath. Of the smooth, calm faces.

"Rested," she says.

Nurse stares at her.

"It is what he said. I let him rest." Her throat is tight. "It is a poor word. But it is the one he used."

For a long moment the old woman does not move. Then she bends, slowly, over the ledger, and the pen scratches once, and again, forty-one times down the column. Bell watches the letters appear, neat and round, one after another, in the faded brown ink.

Rested.

Rested.

Rested.

She sets the pen down at the last line. For a moment the two women stand together in the lamplight, saying nothing, and then Nurse closes the book, and rests both her hands on the cover as though it were warm.

"Thank you," she says.

"I did not do anything."

"You gave me a word," says Nurse. "At my age, that is a great deal."
